Provided that nothing in this subsection shall operate to prevent a minister of the crown from communicating to the Senate or to the House of Commons any information obtained under the provisions of this act.

subtopic: LABOUR AND EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF SEPARATE COMMITTEES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: LABOUR AND EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF SEPARATE COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I should like to make a suggestion to the Prime Minister and the government with regard to the standing committees of the house. I would preface this by saying that in my opinion the present standing committee set-up of this house could be improved. If the suggestion I offer receives the approval of the government, consideration ought to be given to this point before the special committee now preparing the list of members to serve on these committees makes its report to the house.
Two of the most important subjects with which the house must, deal are labour and external -affairs. Under the existing arrangements both these subjects fall within the jurisdiction of one committee, the standing committee on industrial and international relations. At this and succeeding sessions these two subjects must receive far greater attention than has been the custom in the past, and I believe the work is too heavy and too important to be placed upon a single committee. In my opinion there should be two standing committees, one on labour and industrial relations and the other on commonwealth and international affairs. Thus we would be assured of the opportunity for more adequate study by duly constituted committees of both these vital subjects, which have now achieved an importance far greater than at the time the existing committee on industrial and international relations was first established.
Would the Prime Minister and the government give consideration to presenting to the house an amendment to standing order 63 to give effect to this proposal?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: LABOUR AND EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF SEPARATE COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I may say to my hon. friend that the suggestion he has just made

War Appropriation Bills
is one which, if my recollection serves me aright, has been made at previous sessions and I think is one dieserving of very careful consideration. When industrial and international relations were referred to one committee, it was felt that most industrial problems had become more or less world problems, and equally, that the most perplexing of the world problems were related in one way or the other to industry. So it was thought that the committee which would be considering the one subject would naturally be interested in the other. I agree with my hon. friend that at the present time there are no questions more important than those which relate to industry and those which relate to international affairs. If there were two separate committees therefore it might and I believe would improve the opportunities of hon. members to give careful study to these questions. I shall be very happy to consult with my colleagues immediately as to the desirability of instituting two committees instead of one.

subtopic: INCLUSION OF SCHEDULE OF EXPENDITURES IN PRINTED BILL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INCLUSION OF SCHEDULE OF EXPENDITURES IN PRINTED BILL
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question
of the Minister of Finance with respect to item No. 5 on page 12 of the order paper. During war time the government in bringing down the war appropriation, bills has, with a considerable measure of agreement by the house, departed from the usual parliamentary procedure in dealing with money bills. In presenting such bills in the past few years it has been the practice of the Minister of Finance to provide the members of the house with what one might call' a "fluid schedule" which was debated at great length at the resolution stage before the bill was introduced. This schedule, as I understand it, was submitted only as a guide to the house, but was not made a part of the bill introduced. It did not, therefore, restrict the government in the use of the total appropriation. There were, no doubt, reasons for proceeding in that way during war time. Now that the war is over my question to the minister is this:	Will he
not now revert to the usual peace time practice with respect to money bills, and have the schedule of expenditures attached to and printed with the bill? If that procedure is reverted to, the members of the house will have the printed bill before them and the breakdown of expenditures in the form of a schedule to the bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCLUSION OF SCHEDULE OF EXPENDITURES IN PRINTED BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very full and extended consideration was given to the proposal which the hon. member has now put in words. On the earlier occasion it was not made by him, but rather by members within the government itself, and was given full consideration. Eventually we came to the conclusion that it was too early to revert to the practice of itemizing estimates, and that the situation now is scarcely less predictable, with accuracy and certainty, than it is in time of war. It was felt that there must be some power-and a very considerable power-in the changing of plans in respect of expenditures. That is to say, suppose we give the house an indication of our intention to spend, say, $150 million for a certain purpose. It may turn out between now and the end of the fiscal, year that the amount required is only $75 million, but that a larger amount than we now intend to spend for some other purpose will be required..
May I add that the same question must have arisen at the end of the last war. The armistice was on November 11, 1918, and in June of 1919, a date within the fiscal year following the fiscal year in which the war ended, the government of that day decided it would have to continue the practice of providing for some fluidity in respect of intended expenditures. If the leader of the opposition will look at the 1919 statutes he will find there a demobilization appropriation act based upon the same principles as our war appropriation acts, and indeed using the same words as our acts.
I admit at once that just as soon as possible we should get back to a position where items are passed, and where the government is strictly limited in its expenditures to each item passed. As Minister of Finance I should like to see that position resumed at the earliest possible day. It is a protection to the treasury; it is good in principle and it is a right practice to follow. I am quite unable, however, to recommend that we follow it at this moment or at this stage. We are in the middle of the year in which hostilities have ceased, and at this time many of the items we are going to place before the house, while perhaps a little better than guesses, are not what one could call estimates in any true sense of the word. Nothing like the degree of certainty is possible in respect of these estimates that is possible concerning the estimates for civil purposes.
I hope the leader of the opposition will believe that this matter has been approached with a deep sense of responsibility. It has been canvassed with the senior officers of the

Prairie Farm Assistance
various departments, and while there might possibly be a very human desire on their part for a certain freedom in respect of expenditures, yet they have been most sincere in the advice they have given unanimously that this year we should follow the same principle with which we started the fiscal year, namely, that we should have a lump sum appropriation which we can apply to this, that or the other purpose, provided that those purposes are connected with the war.

speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Reconstruction. I sent him notice of my question before eleven o'clock this morning. If so, why?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: CANCELLATION OP MEETING WITH REPRESENTATIVES OP MANAGEMENT AND WORKERS IN STEEL INDUSTRY
speechtext:
For the past several months I have had a number of meetings with representatives of labour from various industries. These meet ings have been arranged by a committee composed of high officials of the several labour congresses and federations of the country. Some weeks ago I held such a meeting to discuss the problems of the steel industry. In the course of the meeting Mr. Millard asked me to arrange a meeting between a group from labour in the steel industry and a group from the industry itself. At some considerable inconvenience I arranged a meeting-and had to use a good deal of persuasion to do it.

It then appeared to me that the purpose of the proposed meeting was undoubtedly political, rather than constructive. subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, September 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. M. Benidickson for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Benidickson) and the seconder (Mr. Langlois) of this motion for an address to His Excellency. I wish to compliment them on their able presentations on their first appearance as members of this house despite the fact that they failed to see any of the shortcomings of the government of the day. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt), I was surprised to notice that last evening the government were ready, in fact seemed eager to have the vote on this motion proceed when there are so many perplexing or vexing questions before the people of this nation and when as yet responsible ministers had not made statements in connection therewith. It has been pointed out that while the address was quite lengthy it is rather vague and I had thought some of the ministers would have made statements on some of these vexing questions.
The first matter I should like to deal with or at least ask questions about is that of meat rationing which was introduced again in this country on September 10, while this parliament was in session and without any statement on the situation being made by any responsible minister of the government. Some reference was made, I think perhaps by accident, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he was answering a question which had been asked on hog production. His remarks will be found on page 24 of Hansard. He stated that there was a great surplus of meat in Canada at the present time and that we were called upon to supply approximately six per cent of the requirements of the devastated countries. One reading that statement could not help gaining the impression that he did not favour meat rationing in this country at this time. I am glad he is in his seat and if I am wrong in my belief I know he will correct me.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: As the press stated, I did not mention rationing at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think anybody reading the remarks of the minister would gain the impression I have mentioned. He is at

liberty to state now whether or not he favours rationing at this time. According to Mr. Donald Gordon, head of the prices control board, who is in charge of rationing, the great surpluses of meat are to be found at the present time in Canada and the United States. I should like to refer to a report in the New York Times of August 18, 1945. The secretary for agriculture, Mr. C. P. Anderson, who I think is recognized as the czar of food controls in the United States of America, is the sole authority in determining the need of civilian rationing. According to this article he has stated that meat rationing might well end this fall because of the cut-backs and the heavy runs of grass-fed cattle in that country.
I want it to be clearly understood that I am heartily in accord with the idea of supplying all the meat and foodstuffs possible to Britain and the devastated countries of the world, but as I have stated no reasonablt explanation has been given to either the producers or the consumers of this country that we are following the proper course to see that these people obtain this much needed meat and foodstuffs. In fact statistics and experience would indicate that meat rationing at this time is an improper course to follow.
It is true that as a result of government policy hog production is down over thirty per cent at this date, but beef cattle production has increased over thirty per cent since 1939. That is the increase which has occurred during the war years. In many cases the producers have found great difficulty in marketing their stock at the various yards throughout the nation. We had meat rationing from May 27, 1943, until February 29, 1944, and during that time processed meat was allowed to accumulate and spoil at the cost of the Canadian taxpayer. It was estimated that more meat was consumed in Canada during that rationing period than had been consumed previously.
Along with other members, I have been receiving telegrams during the last few days. I happen to represent a constituency which is not entirely wheat producing. The people in my constituency are mixed farmers and I would estimate that half of them harvest their crops with the old threshing machine in order to save their straw for their stock. Among other telegrams I received one from a local processor, a butcher, pointing out that the local rationing board had not received any meat coupons for transients. This meant that during this period no farmer in the locality could purchase meat for his threshing crew. One can understand what that would mean during this busy season with the prevailing shortage of man-power.
SEiPTEMBER 12, 1945	113
The Address-Mr. Ross (Souris)
The first thing I did was to get in touch with the office of Mr. Taylor, the food administrator, who had made this announcement to the people of Canada. I was directed from one office to another, about a dozen in rotation, but I finally found a man who said that he understood the local situation and that these coupons should have been there. He assured me yesterday that he would have this matter straightened out through the Winnipeg office. This gives one some idea of the great bureaucratic set-up we have and the enormous number of officials and inspectors employed in the carrying out of such an undertaking. I trust that this matter has been satisfactorily settled and that these people will be able to procure much needed rations. I do not know of anyone more deserving than those who are working long hours in the harvest fields producing other forms of food.
The producers of meat in Canada are extremely anxious to have as much meat as possible go to Britain and the other devastated countries in order that future markets may be established. However, they do not consider that meat rationing is the proper course to follow at this time and they are vitally concerned. We could better supply that demand on a quota basis rather than, have this rationing set-up.
During the past summer and early autumn we had strikes in the packing plants across Canada which lasted for many days. During that time no meat was processed for anyone in this country or overseas. The government of the day took no action whatever. The producer who happened to have stock at the yards during that period took his trimming when settlement was made for the cattle or hogs. During those days national selective service failed miserably.
Under our prices set-up for beef why should the producer have to take at least one and one-half cents per pound less in early August for animals which had grown and were in better condition as compared with what he would have received early in July? That is what occurred at the various markets across the country and I imagine it may be worse before snow falls this winter. During the past few years there has been a racket in our marketing policy which has affected the level of prices paid to producers of meat.
The Minister of Agriculture was requested t.o institute a permit system covering exports to the United' States of America in case there should be a heavy live stock rim. This could be done quite satisfactorily on the same basis as export permits are granted for barley and oats being shipped to the United States. The
differences in price are very great, usually at least fifty per cent more being paid there than is received in Canada, but that difference could be pooled for the producers. It would be very simple to handle and the producer would not be taking the licking that he has been forced to take every time these runs occur in the yards throughout this country. By so doing we would preserve our price control system for the Canadian consumer, so that no fault could be found in that respect. I believe that some such provision as this should be made immediately. As I have pointed out, we have over thirty per cent more cattle in the country to-day than at the beginning of the war, and many of our farmers will be forced this fall by force of circumstances to market almost their entire herds in certain parts of the west. Therefore it is imperative that some such step as I have proposed be taken for their protection.
We should also endeavour to obtain world markets. If we go along much further as we have been doing, the United States and other markets will be lost to the producers of this country.
As I have said, this is a vexed problem for many people in Canada, both producers and consumers, and a statement should be made by a responsible minister of the crown before we are asked to vote on this motion. We should not be asked to content ourselves with statements made by people, many of whom might not be able to have themselves elected under a democratic form of government such as we have in this country. The war is over, whether it has been declared over or not, and our people expect something different. They expect to hear from their democratic representatives.
A few words on another matter. It is quite apparent, despite all the government propaganda about its reconstruction plans, propaganda put out, by the way, at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer, that the government's plans are at this date non-existent.
My colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), in speaking of demobilization yesterday, gave emphatic proof of the unfairness of the present demobilization system, especially with reference to the overseas men who have done so much for us during the past five years and more. He also pointed out how the present system of demobilization operates to the advantage of many of the members of our second army, the N.R.M.A. men, which I think is unfortunate.
At one period of the war men in the army were allowed upon discharge a clothing allowance at $35; later on, the clothing allowance
The Address-Mr. Ross (Souris)

was raised to $65, and at the present time it is $100. I sincerely trust that the government will see that all the men discharged eventually receive the same clothing allowance. I think that can justly be expected of the government.
With respect to members of the armed forces wishing to take university training it is recognized in my province at least, that grade 12 is the equivalent of first year at university, and in my little town-and the same is true of many towns in the province-grade 12 is taught in collegiate. But we had a statement from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott) the other day that grade 12 will not be recognized as first year at university, and that these men must attend the university.
I noticed a statement in this morning's press by the president of the great university of Toronto that over 900 applications had been received to attend that university this fall, 600 of which were from the armed services. He said that they could accommodate only 400. Therefore I urge, Mr. Speaker, that this matter be reconsidered and that these young men be allowed to take their first year university training in their own home districts. Many of them are young chaps with no position to support them and, if this suggestion were adopted and they could take their first year's training at home, their parents would not be out of pocket for their son's living expenses.
I wish to refer to national housing. As was so well said by my leader, the present situation is a blot on the record of the government, and worse. In the prairie provinces, outside of the large cities, it is an absolute washout. The finance companies, and the insurance companies whom the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has been consulting, refuse point blank to have anything to do under the act with housing in the towns and villages of the prairie provinces, so that the plan is entirely inoperative in any shape or form outside of the large cities. Tliat is true of every town and village west of the great lakes, where there is an urgent demand for housing to-day. Canada's housing requirements are probably half a million houses short of being met to-day. We have national housing under the Minister of Finance and we have wartime housing under the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). It has been charged in recent days by responsible lumbermen that certain finishing materials have been frozen for wartime housing, where the material is actually not required as yet. If that is the case these materials should be released. In my neighbourhood-and I think the same is true all across the country-many people have begun to build their homes which they intended to occupy this winter, and now they find they 
cannot proceed to make them habitable for the winter months because of lack of materials. That is a very serious problem for many people. In the three prairie provinces seventy per cent of the population is rural; yet under our controller system there is a priority for the cities of the prairies of 70 per cent of the lumber available. The whole thing is just wrong end to. The result is that the individual cannot get the finishing materials which he urgently requires at this time, and some statement clarifying the situation should be made by a responsible minister. I trust that the responsible minister will be able to do something toward decentralization in this matter. Centralization seems to be growing in every department of the government, but now that the war is over, theoretically at least, it is time that we moved toward decentralization in many government undertakings, and the government should at least tell the people what they may expect in the matter of housing during the coming months and in the nearfuture years because the people are much perturbed over the present situation.
Another matter on which I should like to say a few words is the transferable vote, and this is a personal thought of my own. I know there is difference of opinion in all groups about the transferable vote. When the Prime Minister accepted the leadership of his party in 1919 he set forth in his chart the subject of election reform. It is passing strange that at this late date he has made no move in that respect. He has told us that this is his last parliament, and yet no move has been made by him to institute the transferable vote in our dominion elections. We have had the transferable vote in Manitoba for many years and it has worked most satisfactorily there. They have it in Alberta also, I think, and it has worked well there too. In a democracy such as ours surely the will of the majority should prevail to the fullest possible extent. But what happens under our present system? In the last dominion parliament we had seventy-four members who were elected on a minority vote. In this parliament we have 149 members who were elected on a minority vote. Provision should be made in our election machinery for the transferable vote, so that where a number of candidates are contesting a riding the voter can indicate his second choice and the will of the majority of the electors prevail. I have always thought we should have that in a democracy such as ours, and I trust that the government will do something along this line.
I was surprised at the way in which the Prime Minister wandered around in his remark? the other day, following the speech

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
so ably delivered by my leader. I could understand, of course, that the right hon. gentleman might be very tired after the load he has carried. Nevertheless I had expected more of the Prime Minister than what we heard. He spoke of having received his second mandate, although he did not go into detail and tell us how he had received it. True enough, his party received more votes than any other group, but they received very far from a majority of the votes. He did not tell us of the appeals he had made to sectionalism, both during the war years and during the campaign, pitting the wishes of certain sections of the country against those of others. I am very proud of my leader; he conducted a statesmanlike campaign from coast to coast in Canada; he was prepared to stand or fall by his principles as a great Canadian. Of that I am very proud, and I would be just as proud had I been defeated in my riding.
As to the soldiers' vote, they were so confused, that the vast majority of them never cast a ballot. I can understand that to some extent. The government in power, with their propaganda at the expense of the taxpayer, and their set-up to get it across to the troops, so befogged many of the soldiers that, as I say, the majority failed to cast a ballot at all. I am very happy to be able to point out that, despite the government propaganda, I for some reason received a complete majority over both of my opponents, as did my leader, the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken).
I think I should follow the example of the leaders of the groups and endeavour to be brief on this occasion. But there are some vexing problems before the people at the present time, and I again appeal to the responsible ministers to make some statements on them for our guidance.
I shall support the amendment moved by my leader. I will not take time to read it; it will be found on page 34 of Hansard. I do not believe that any member of the house of any group dare stand up and tell his constituents that he is opposed to any one of the three sections of the amendment and that he is satisfied with the efforts of the government in any one of these three respects. Therefore, if they are to vote conscientiously, no matter where they sit in this house they should support the amendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The speech of His Excellency delivered at the opening of this parliament has received some criticism and some praise. There is, however,
one paragraph in it on which all hon. members can agree, that is the first paragraph, which reads:
You will rejoice with me that the opening of the twentieth parliament of Canada comes at the moment of the victorious conclusion of the war.
I believe that not only all the members of this house but all the people of Canada and the peoples of the united nations who, with us, carried on this victorious conflict rejoice at the ending of the war.
However, it seems to me that our rejoicing is not complete. Our people are not entirely happy. They have fears and forebodings, which were discernible for a. considerable time before the war ended. The men and women in the services and the men and women in the war industries were hoping for the end of the war, but fearful of what was going to happen to them when the war ended; and I submit to you, sir, that if we consider the. ten years preceding this war, and the fact that the men and women who went into our armed forces and into our war industries were recruited in the main from that section of our population which came to maturity in the ten years prior to 1939, it is no wonder that they were fearful of what they would come back to when the war was over.
I think, although perhaps he did not intend it in that way, that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) in his forceful speech yesterday evening proved this point, although he did not draw from it the full conclusion that he should have drawn. He said, as reported in yesterday's Hansard, at page 105:
What we do need, and wThat we have not had in my adult life-and what I fear we can never have from this government-is "action'' to give us full employment.
I do not know my hon. friend's age, but I imagine it is somewhere between thirty-five and forty. Consequently his adult life was not only in that period when this government was in office but also in the period when his own party was in office, and the full employment we are looking for to-day was just as far distant then as it is to-day.
That brings me to the next point I wish to make, and that is that this war, the last one, and the period in between the two wars have proven one thing, and proven it beyond the possibility of a doubt, namely, that the capitalist system can give full employment only in time of war; it has never given full employment in time of peace, and it never can give full employment in time of peace because its operation depends upon a reservoir of unemployment to keep it going.

I accept the compliment, but I still insist. I have in my hands a copy of the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance for the year 1943; and in the section where he refers to our victory bond sales he says this:

I think that is conclusive. That is not the full sentence; I will read the rest of the sentence, which gives us another sidelight on the capitalist system which is no better, indeed, but perhaps worse than the one I have already mentioned. But it is strange that we had to have a war in order that our people might be able to set a little bit aside for that rainy day which we are told always comes at some time in our lives. The next part of the sentence is this:
. . . and it is apparent that some high pressure promoters of dubious or worthless securities are attempting to exploit these savings.
That is capitalism.
I shall touch briefly on two or three points in the speech from the throne. The first item with Which I wish to deal is the paragraph which reads:
Preparations for the demobilization, rehabilitation and reestablishment in civil life of the men and women in the armed forces were well under way when Germany surrendered. The same is true of measures for the reconversion of the economic life of our country from a war-time to a peace-time basis, and for the maintenance of a high level of employment and national income. The plans thus developed to meet the requirements of the period of transition are now being put into full operation.
There is something wrong here. That paragraph is either a mis-statement of facts or the references that we hear throughout the country to the unpreparedness of the government, and the references that have been made in this house, are not correct. I maintain that this paragraph is a gross misrepresentation of the facts as they now are. As a matter of fact the government has no plans and it cannot
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
have any plans on the procedure that it is following, because it does not take under its control or direction the economic life of this country on which depends the reestablishment of the returned men and the full employment and prosperity of our people.
In the copy of "Post-war Planning Information" which came to my office yesterday the government gives its objectives as high and stable employment and income, and a greater sense of public responsibility for individual economic security and welfare. Here is what they say:
(1)	To facilitate private enterprise to produce and provide employment.
I want hon. members to note the wording of that statement. It is not employment that the people of this country need. What they need is production; but we are going back to the psychology of the nineteen thirties. We are thinking in terms of employment and not in terms of the things that people work for. Let us look at the different attitude that was adopted during the war. We got full employment during the war, but we did not get full employment by trying to provide jobs for people; we got full employment by providing the needs of the war. I submit to you, sir, that we can never get full employment in Canada by just thinking of making jobs for people. We have to think in terms of the people's needs and then plan and organize to fulfil those needs. If we do that, we shall have full employment; and when there are no needs to be filled, if people are unemployed so much the better.
The other objectives are:
(2)	To promote bold action by the state in those fields in which the public interest calls for public enterprise in national development;
(3)	To provide, through public investment, productive employment for our human and physical resources when international and other conditions adversely affect employment; and
(4)	To provide, on a basis of small regular payments against large and uncertain individual risks, for such hazards and disabilities as unemployment, sickness and old age.
I tell you, sir, that the government can never meet the situation that confronts us at the present time with a policy of that kind. The hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard said last night that laissez-Saire was dead. I go further than that and say that the capitalist system is dead. It reminds me of the old nursery rhyme:
Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall,
Humpty Dumpty had a great fall.
All the king's horses and all the king's men Couldn't put Humpty together again.
And we are not going to put it together again with a policy of that kind.

If the ministers could only get together before they begin contradicting me, rather than after, we would make much better progress. The conference they are now holding should have been held before they came into the chamber. In any event I shall leave the matter there.
The next point I should like to discuss is that of housing. I am not going to deal with it at any length, because it has been dealt with by several hon. members. It was referred to by my leader, and undoubtedly further reference will be made to the subject in the house, unless something is done very quickly.
So far as housing is concerned, conditions in Vancouver are deplorable. Housing conditions in most cities of Canada were bad before the war. They have continually become worse. I am not blaming the government for that, because it was inevitable that that condition should develop. In British Columbia, since the beginning of the war there has been a great increase in population. From 1941, when the census was taken, to 1944, the population increased from 818,000 in the earlier year to an estimated 932,000 in the latter year. It is considered that over 60,000 of those people are settled in Vancouver. The situation grows worse daily as many of the men from the armed services who enlisted in other provinces are taking their discharge in British Columbia, or are coming to that province after being discharged. That happened after the last war, and it is happening again this time.
The government is leaving the matter of housing to private enterprise. I hold in my hand a news item from the Vancouver Daily Province, dated July 16, which says, "Ilsley introduces vast scheme to provide veterans' homes. Ottawa guarantees builders against loss." I thought my friends favoured private enterprise, and urged that private enterprise had a right to its profit because it was prepared to take risks. But the private enterprise we have to-day asks the government to take the risks while it takes the profits. Surely that is a poor sort of private enterprise. And when it reaches that stage I say it ceases to be private enterprise and should receive no further consideration from anyone.
When during the war we needed so many planes, so many tanks, so many ships and so many guns the government planned for the production of them. So far as it was able it did not permit anything to interfere with that production-and it had wonderful success, bur when veterans need homes, when war workers need homes, when our people generally need homes, why in the world can we not decide how many homes we need, and then plan and organize to build them? Why should we leave those things to private enterprise, while we guarantee them against loss, if they should have any, and at the same time permit them to take a profit, if there is one? We cannot carry on the business of making provision for our people that way.
In the short time remaining to me may I make the admission that perhaps the reason for the mental gymnastics of which the Minister of Labour complained a few minutes ago is that I have been trying to understand the social and economic philosophy of the official opposition. During the election and since that time I thought they wanted the removal of controls, and a return to private enterprise so fast that it would make one's hair stand on end. But since coming to parliament and listening to them I have decided that their tune has changed. Perhaps when I say that I am not altogether correct. In my view they have two tunes, if I have caught the strains correctly, one of which is entitled Throw the Controls out of the Window, and the second of which is Let the Government Get Action. But they cannot have both. The authority which is going to get action must have control. If we want the government to act-and this group does want it, and is willing to give the government the authority and control for action-it must have control. But hon. members to my right want it both ways. I should like to quote their position as it was placed before the house last night by the hon.
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt'). This is what he says as reported on page 107 of Hansard:
The end of laissez-faire means another thing. It means that the government are no longer solely the administrators of the affairs of this country; that they can be content just to let things go. The government are ultimately responsible for every part of our national life, and there is no ill which befalls the people of this country which it is not the duty of the government to correct. If they are to correct all those ills, they must get a new outlook.
Somewhat earlier in his address-and as I said before, his maiden speech was a good one-the hon. member said we do not want a new social order. Now it seems we must have a new outlook without a new social order.
